claim: PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 are the two most important high-affinity phosphate transporters required for up to 75% of Pi uptake in Arabidopsis.
source: PHT1;1 and PHT1;4, the two most important high-affinity phosphate transporters required for up to 75% of Pi uptake in Arabidopsis, are localized to the distal part of the root tip (Shin et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shin et al., 2004.

claim: PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 are localized to the distal part of the root tip.
source: PHT1;1 and PHT1;4, the two most important high-affinity phosphate transporters required for up to 75% of Pi uptake in Arabidopsis, are localized to the distal part of the root tip (Shin et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shin et al., 2004.

claim: PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 are expressed in the root tip (primarily in the root cap) at the transcriptional and protein levels.
source: Both transporters are observed in the root tip (primarily in the root cap), where they are expressed at the transcriptional and protein levels (Figure 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A showing reporter lines expressing transcriptional and translational fusions for PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 localized in the root cap.

claim: PHF1 is expressed in the root tip (primarily in the root cap) at the transcriptional and protein levels.
source: Both transporters are observed in the root tip (primarily in the root cap), where they are expressed at the transcriptional and protein levels (Figure 1A) with PHF1, a crucial component facilitating PHT1 post-translational regulation and its targeting to the PM (Gonzalez et al., 2005; Bayle et al., 2011) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and citations to Gonzalez et al., 2005 and Bayle et al., 2011.

claim: PHF1 is a crucial component facilitating PHT1 post-translational regulation and its targeting to the plasma membrane.
source: with PHF1, a crucial component facilitating PHT1 post-translational regulation and its targeting to the PM (Gonzalez et al., 2005; Bayle et al., 2011) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gonzalez et al., 2005 and Bayle et al., 2011.

claim: 33Pi accumulation was observed at the extremity of the root tip when fed to plantlets.
source: When fed to plantlets, 33Pi accumulation was observed at the extremity of the root tip (Figure 1B), including the meristematic zone (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B showing accumulation of 33P in the root tip.

claim: 33Pi accumulation was observed in the meristematic zone.
source: When fed to plantlets, 33Pi accumulation was observed at the extremity of the root tip (Figure 1B), including the meristematic zone (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Pi translocation absorbed by the whole root system contributes to the presence of Pi in the root tip.
source: Pi translocation absorbed by the whole root system contributes to the presence of Pi in the root tip, as revealed by the accumulation of radiotracer in the root tip within 30 min of 33Pi application to the middle of the root system (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing 33P in the root tip 30 min after application to the middle of the root.

claim: Radiotracer accumulates in the root tip within 30 min of 33Pi application to the middle of the root system.
source: Pi translocation absorbed by the whole root system contributes to the presence of Pi in the root tip, as revealed by the accumulation of radiotracer in the root tip within 30 min of 33Pi application to the middle of the root system (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The uptake of phosphate relies on a family of nine high-affinity transporters identified as PHT1 in Arabidopsis.
source: The uptake of phosphate (Pi), an essential plant macronutrient, relies on a family of nine high-affinity transporters, identified as PHT1 in the plant model Arabidopsis (Nussaume et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nussaume et al., 2011.

claim: Mineral nutrition is classically associated with the root epidermis.
source: Mineral nutrition is classically associated with the root epidermis, and the various PHT1 members were identified within this cell layer (Mudge et al., 2002; Karthikeyan et al., 2002; Misson et al., 2004; Nussaume et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Various PHT1 members were identified within the root epidermis cell layer.
source: Mineral nutrition is classically associated with the root epidermis, and the various PHT1 members were identified within this cell layer (Mudge et al., 2002; Karthikeyan et al., 2002; Misson et al., 2004; Nussaume et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mudge et al., 2002; Karthikeyan et al., 2002; Misson et al., 2004; Nussaume et al., 2011.

claim: PHT1 transporters are particularly abundant where hair cells develop.
source: These transporters are particularly abundant where hair cells develop (Daram et al., 1998; Brady et al., 2007), as this increases the surface area in contact with the environment and improves nutrient uptake (Peret et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Daram et al., 1998 and Brady et al., 2007.

claim: Hair cell development increases the surface area in contact with the environment and improves nutrient uptake.
source: These transporters are particularly abundant where hair cells develop (Daram et al., 1998; Brady et al., 2007), as this increases the surface area in contact with the environment and improves nutrient uptake (Peret et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Peret et al., 2011.

claim: Transcriptomic analyses of specific root cell layers revealed the accumulation of PHT1 transporters in the root tip.
source: Transcriptomic analyses of specific root cell layers (Birnbaum et al., 2003) and analysis of the PHT1 expression pattern has revealed the accumulation of these transporters in the root tip (Mudge et al., 2002; Karthikeyan et al., 2002; Misson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Birnbaum et al., 2003; Mudge et al., 2002; Karthikeyan et al., 2002; Misson et al., 2004.

claim: Expression of FCY-UPP in the root cap combined with 5FC treatment abolished the 33Pi accumulation observed in either the WT or the transgenic line not treated with 5FC.
source: Expression of FCY-UPP in the root cap combined with 5FC treatment clearly abolished the 33Pi accumulation observed in either the WT or the transgenic line not treated with 5FC.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating abolished Pi accumulation in the Q0171>>FCY-UPP line treated with 5FC.

claim: Treating the WT line with 5FC had no effect on either plant growth or Pi accumulation.
source: Treating the WT line with 5FC had no effect on either plant growth (results not shown) or Pi accumulation, demonstrating its innocuous nature when FCY-UPP is not expressed (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There exists an active Pi uptake process at the root cap level.
source: This result establishes the existence of an unexpected active Pi uptake process at the root cap level.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing abolished Pi accumulation when root cap is inactivated.

claim: Arrested root growth was observed within 2 days of 5FC treatment in the FCY-UPP-based system.
source: Nevertheless, this FCY-UPP-based system cannot be used to quantify the physiological effect of root cap ablation on Pi status, since arrested root growth was observed within 2 days of 5FC treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The phf1-1 mutant exhibits a 70–80% reduction in Pi uptake.
source: We used a PHF1 mutant (phf1-1) to circumvent this obstacle, as this mutation strongly reduces PHT1 accumulation in the PM, resulting in a 70–80% reduction in Pi uptake (Bayle et al., 2011; Gonzalez et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bayle et al., 2011 and Gonzalez et al., 2005.

claim: The phf1-1 mutation strongly reduces PHT1 accumulation in the plasma membrane.
source: We used a PHF1 mutant (phf1-1) to circumvent this obstacle, as this mutation strongly reduces PHT1 accumulation in the PM, resulting in a 70–80% reduction in Pi uptake (Bayle et al., 2011; Gonzalez et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bayle et al., 2011 and Gonzalez et al., 2005.

claim: The phf1-1 mutant exhibits phosphate starvation traits in Pi-rich medium.
source: Consequently, the phf1-1 mutant exhibits phosphate starvation traits in Pi-rich medium, although its growth is only slightly reduced.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the reduced Pi uptake in the mutant.

claim: The growth of the phf1-1 mutant is only slightly reduced.
source: Consequently, the phf1-1 mutant exhibits phosphate starvation traits in Pi-rich medium, although its growth is only slightly reduced.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of the mutant phenotype.

claim: PHT1;4-mCherry fusion protein colocalizes with the PM-specific FM4-64 dye.
source: The proper targeting of the PHT1;4-mCherry fusion protein was validated by its colocalization with the PM-specific FM4-64 dye (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: An effective restoration of PHT1 targeting in the root cap PM has taken place in the phf1 Q0171>>PHF1 line.
source: This confirms that an effective restoration of PHT1 targeting in the root cap PM has taken place in the phf1 Q0171>>PHF1 line (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: A very low, diffuse fluorescence signal could be detected in other tissues corresponding to a low level of ER-retained protein in the phf1-1 mutant.
source: A very low, diffuse fluorescence signal could also be detected in other tissues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), corresponding to a previously reported low level of ER-retained protein in the phf1-1 mutant (Gonzalez et al., 2005; Bayle et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and citations to Gonzalez et al., 2005 and Bayle et al., 2011.

claim: Rapid Pi absorption occurs after only 1 min following 33P addition.
source: Our time course experiment revealed rapid Pi absorption after only 1 min following 33P addition (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Full restoration of Pi absorption at the phf1Q0171>>PHF1 root tip similar to the WT level was observed.
source: We observed full restoration of Pi absorption at the phf1Q0171>>PHF1 root tip similar to the WT level, whereas no labeling was detected in the phf1-1 mutant during the same time period (Figure 2B,C), demonstrating the successful functional complementation of Pi uptake activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: No labeling was detected in the phf1-1 mutant during the same time period as WT and phf1Q0171>>PHF1.
source: We observed full restoration of Pi absorption at the phf1Q0171>>PHF1 root tip similar to the WT level, whereas no labeling was detected in the phf1-1 mutant during the same time period (Figure 2B,C), demonstrating the successful functional complementation of Pi uptake activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: WT plants exhibited a very low level of radiotracer in the region between the root tip and mature zone (corresponding to the elongation and differentiation zones; approximately 500–900 µm from the apex).
source: WT plants exhibited a very low level of radiotracer (Figure 2D) in the region between these two parts of the root (corresponding to the elongation and differentiation zones; approximately 500–900 µm from the apex), indicating poor Pi absorption activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The elongation and differentiation zones show poor Pi absorption activity.
source: WT plants exhibited a very low level of radiotracer (Figure 2D) in the region between these two parts of the root (corresponding to the elongation and differentiation zones; approximately 500–900 µm from the apex), indicating poor Pi absorption activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the low radiotracer signal in this region.

claim: Root labeling occurs in the differentiated zone (≥1.2 mm from the root tip) as a result of uptake through the epidermis.
source: Root labeling occurs in the differentiated zone (≥1.2 mm from the root tip) as a result of uptake through the epidermis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of radiotracer accumulation shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The signal present in the WT was impaired in both phf1-1 and phf1Q0171>>PHF1.
source: The signal present in the WT was impaired in both phf1-1 and phf1Q0171>>PHF1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The 33P quantification describes a specific enrichment in the phf1Q0171>>PHF1 root tip.
source: This confirms the specificity of the root cap complementation in phf1Q0171>>PHF1, since the 33P quantification only describes a specific enrichment in the phf1Q0171>>PHF1 root tip (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the WT, the accumulation of P33 was high in the root tip.
source: Similarly, in the WT, the accumulation of P33 was high in the root tip.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Reduced growth in the aerial parts is a well-known consequence of Pi starvation.
source: Reduced growth in the aerial parts is a well-known consequence of Pi starvation.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Reduced growth in the aerial parts is conserved in the phf1-1 mutant even in Pi-rich medium.
source: This feature is conserved in the phf1-1 mutant (Gonzalez et al., 2005) even in Pi-rich medium, in agreement with the low Pi-status of these plants.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gonzalez et al., 2005.

claim: The root architectures of phf1-1 and the WT were similar in Pi-rich medium.
source: By contrast, the root architectures of phf1-1 (Thibaud et al., 2010) and the WT were similar in Pi-rich medium, confirming that root growth responds to external Pi (Svistoonoff et al., 2007; Peret et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Thibaud et al., 2010; Svistoonoff et al., 2007; Peret et al., 2011.

claim: Root growth responds to external Pi.
source: By contrast, the root architectures of phf1-1 (Thibaud et al., 2010) and the WT were similar in Pi-rich medium, confirming that root growth responds to external Pi (Svistoonoff et al., 2007; Peret et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Svistoonoff et al., 2007 and Peret et al., 2011.

claim: Free Pi measured in roots or leaves of the complemented line was similar to the phf1-1 mutant.
source: Free Pi measured in roots or leaves of the complemented line was similar to the phf1-1 mutant, indicating full metabolization of the excess absorbed Pi (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The excess absorbed Pi in the complemented line is fully metabolized.
source: Free Pi measured in roots or leaves of the complemented line was similar to the phf1-1 mutant, indicating full metabolization of the excess absorbed Pi (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similar free Pi levels despite increased uptake.

claim: The phf1J0481>>PHF1 line fully restored Pi uptake to a level similar to that of the WT.
source: As expected, the phf1J0481>>PHF1 line fully restored Pi uptake to a level similar to that of the WT.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Pi uptake in phf1Q0171>>PHF1 and phf1J1092>>PHF1 restored 20% of the difference in Pi uptake between the WT control and the phf1-1 mutant.
source: By contrast, Pi uptake in phf1Q0171>>PHF1 and phf1J1092>>PHF1 restored 20% of the difference in Pi uptake between the WT control and the phf1-1 mutant (Figure 3B, Figure 3B—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The root cap contributes approximately 20% of the total amount of Pi absorbed from the medium by the roots.
source: Our results indicate that the root cap contributes approximately 20% of the total amount of Pi absorbed from the medium by the roots.
evidence: This claim is based on data from the complementation experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The phf1-1 mutant probably displays residual activity in the root cap tissue.
source: It is likely that this value slightly underestimates the root cap's contribution to Pi uptake, as the phf1-1 mutant probably displays residual activity in this tissue.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about potential underestimation.

claim: Rosette weight of in vitro plantlets was increased in all three complemented lines as compared to the phf1-1 mutant after transfer from Pi-depleted to Pi-rich medium during 4 days.
source: Rosette weight of in vitro plantlets was increased in all three complemented lines (as compared to the phf1-1 mutant, Figure 3C, Figure 3C—source data 1) after transfer from Pi-depleted to Pi-rich medium during 4 days.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The root cap complementation restored 40% of the growth in phf1Q0171>>PHF1 and phf1J1092>>PHF1 lines.
source: The root cap complementation restored 40% of the growth (phf1Q0171>>PHF1 and phf1J1092>>PHF1 lines) and in agreement with the full restoration of Pi uptake similar to the WT control, the phf1J0481>>PHF1 line does not present any growth defects.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The phf1J0481>>PHF1 line does not present any growth defects.
source: The root cap complementation restored 40% of the growth (phf1Q0171>>PHF1 and phf1J1092>>PHF1 lines) and in agreement with the full restoration of Pi uptake similar to the WT control, the phf1J0481>>PHF1 line does not present any growth defects.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The rosette biomass of the phf1Q0171>>PHF1 line exhibited a significant 80% increase in rosette biomass, as compared to the phf1-1 mutant, when grown on sand hydroponically with 10 µM Pi supply for 3 to 4 weeks.
source: The rosette biomass of the phf1Q0171>>PHF1 line (in which complementation was restricted to the root tip) exhibited a significant 80% increase in rosette biomass, as compared to the phf1-1 mutant (Table 1, Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: The gain in biomass of the root cap-complemented line reached 180% when compared to the phf1-1 mutant in soil experiments after 6 weeks of development.
source: In this case, the gain in biomass of the root cap-complemented line turned out to be even higher, reaching 180% (Table 1) when compared to the phf1-1 mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: The complemented lines (phf1J1092>>PHF1, phf1Q0171>>PHF1 and phf1J0481>>PHF1) lost the strong induction of PHT1;4-GUS expression observed in the phf1-2 mutant when Pi is present in the growth medium.
source: As a consequence, the complemented lines (phf1J1092>>PHF1, phf1Q0171>>PHF1 and phf1J0481>>PHF1) lost the strong induction of PHT1;4-GUS expression observed in the phf1-2 mutant when Pi is present in the growth medium.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Most of the markers regulated by external phosphate were not affected, and were observed to react identically in WT, phf1-1 and phf1Q0171>>PHF1 backgrounds.
source: Most of the markers regulated by external phosphate were not affected, and were observed to react identically in WT, phf1-1 and phf1Q0171>>PHF1 backgrounds (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: A general repression of systemically regulated Pi starvation-induced genes occurred after transfer of the WT and phf1Q0171>>PHF1 lines into Pi-rich medium after 3 days.
source: Analysis of the systemically regulated Pi starvation-induced genes revealed a different situation, in which a general repression of these markers occurred after transfer of the WT and phf1Q0171>>PHF1 lines into Pi-rich medium after 2 days (results not shown) or 3 days (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Systemic markers are strongly induced when the phf1-1 mutant line is grown in high Pi.
source: As previously reported (Gonzalez et al., 2005), these systemic markers are strongly induced when the phf1-1 mutant line is grown in high Pi (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B), whereas these genes are repressed in the WT.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, and a citation to Gonzalez et al., 2005.

claim: The repression of the systemically regulated genes was partially rescued in the root cap PHF1-complemented line.
source: The repression of the systemically regulated genes was partially rescued in the root cap PHF1-complemented line.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The repression of systemically regulated genes in the root cap PHF1-complemented line was equivalent to half the repression observed in the WT.
source: This repression was equivalent to half the repression observed in the WT.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: There exists a non-proportional relationship between Pi uptake, growth and systemic regulation.
source: This is not proportional to the additional Pi uptake related to root cap complementation (at least 20%), confirming the existence of a non-proportional relationship between Pi uptake, growth and systemic regulation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that 20% increase in Pi uptake leads to 50% repression of systemic markers.

claim: Clear labeling of the root cap was observed in rice by applying a short pulse of 33P radiotracer.
source: Clear labeling of the root cap was observed in these specimens by applying the aforementioned protocol consisting of a short pulse of 33P radiotracer (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Clear labeling of the root cap was observed in Lotus japonicus by applying a short pulse of 33P radiotracer.
source: Clear labeling of the root cap was observed in these specimens by applying the aforementioned protocol consisting of a short pulse of 33P radiotracer (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The migration of Pi is clearly visible in rice beginning at the extremity of the root tip (1 min labeling) and moving gradually toward the differentiated tissues of the root (after 3 and 5 min).
source: The migration of Pi is clearly visible in both plants beginning at the extremity of the root tip (1 min labeling) and moving gradually toward the differentiated tissues of the root (after 3 and 5 min in rice and lotus; Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The migration of Pi is clearly visible in lotus beginning at the extremity of the root tip (1 min labeling) and moving gradually toward the differentiated tissues of the root (after 3 and 5 min).
source: The migration of Pi is clearly visible in both plants beginning at the extremity of the root tip (1 min labeling) and moving gradually toward the differentiated tissues of the root (after 3 and 5 min in rice and lotus; Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pi uptake takes place in the root cap in rice.
source: The quantification of 33P after 1 min (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) indicates that Pi uptake takes place in the root cap, as in Arabidopsis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Pi uptake takes place in the root cap in Lotus japonicus.
source: The quantification of 33P after 1 min (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) indicates that Pi uptake takes place in the root cap, as in Arabidopsis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pi uptake at the root tip is a feature shared by several disparate plant species.
source: These results provide evidence that Pi uptake at the root tip is a feature shared by several disparate plant species.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of root cap Pi uptake in Arabidopsis, rice, and Lotus japonicus.

claim: The Arabidopsis root cap appears to be a 'hot spot' for Pi absorption, despite its small surface area.
source: The Arabidopsis root cap therefore appears to be a "hot spot" for Pi absorption, despite its small surface area.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing significant Pi uptake by the small root cap tissue.

claim: Nehemiah Grew drew a connection between plant nutrition and the distal end of the root tip.
source: Interestingly, this confirms the hypothesis of the 17th century plant anatomist Nehemiah Grew, who drew a connection between plant nutrition and the distal end of the root tip (Grew, 1682).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Grew, 1682.

claim: At the root tip, only the cap seems to play an important role in Pi acquisition.
source: At the root tip, only the cap seems to play an important role in Pi acquisition.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing high Pi uptake in the cap but not in the elongation zone.

claim: The elongation zone displays poor Pi absorption despite its essential metabolic activity.
source: Indeed, the elongation zone (distal to the cap) displays poor Pi absorption despite its essential metabolic activity.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The fast rate of root growth reduces the period spent by cells in the elongation zone by 6 to 7 hr.
source: For instance, the fast rate of root growth reduces the period spent by cells in this area by 6 to 7 hr (Beemster and Baskin, 1998), limiting the time allocated to protein production.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Beemster and Baskin, 1998.

claim: The fast rate of root growth limits the time allocated to protein production in the elongation zone.
source: For instance, the fast rate of root growth reduces the period spent by cells in this area by 6 to 7 hr (Beemster and Baskin, 1998), limiting the time allocated to protein production.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the short time cells spend in the elongation zone.

claim: The cell elongation process could contribute to diluting the activity of the produced PHT1 transporters.
source: Additionally, the cell elongation process in this region could contribute to diluting the activity of the produced PHT1 transporters.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the effect of cell elongation.

claim: The root cap is located below the elongation and meristematic zones of the root.
source: These features do not affect the root cap, which is located below the elongation and meristematic zones of the root and is composed of cells that are 10 to 20 times smaller than mature epidermis cells (Beemster and Baskin, 1998) and that have low turn-over (Dolan et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Root cap cells are 10 to 20 times smaller than mature epidermis cells.
source: These features do not affect the root cap, which is located below the elongation and meristematic zones of the root and is composed of cells that are 10 to 20 times smaller than mature epidermis cells (Beemster and Baskin, 1998) and that have low turn-over (Dolan et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Beemster and Baskin, 1998.

claim: Root cap cells have low turn-over.
source: These features do not affect the root cap, which is located below the elongation and meristematic zones of the root and is composed of cells that are 10 to 20 times smaller than mature epidermis cells (Beemster and Baskin, 1998) and that have low turn-over (Dolan et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dolan et al., 1993.

claim: The small size and low turn-over of root cap cells likely contributes to the high cellular concentration of PHT1 proteins in the membrane of this tissue.
source: This likely contributes to the high cellular concentration of PHT1 proteins in the membrane of this tissue.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the characteristics of root cap cells.

claim: The root cap structure of Arabidopsis is composed of 180–260 cells.
source: The root cap structure of Arabidopsis, composed of 180–260 cells (Dolan et al., 1993), can appear simple in comparison to other plant species.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dolan et al., 1993.

claim: There are as many as 4,000–21,000 cells in the maize root cap.
source: For example, there are as many as 4,000–21,000 cells in the maize root cap (Clowes, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clowes, 1976.

claim: Maize has 20 cell layers in the columella.
source: This disparity can be explained by the presence of additional cell layers in the columella, with 20 in maize (Iijima et al., 2008) and 16 in rice plantlets (Wang et al., 2014a), in comparison to only 5 in Arabidopsis (Dolan et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Iijima et al., 2008.

claim: Rice plantlets have 16 cell layers in the columella.
source: This disparity can be explained by the presence of additional cell layers in the columella, with 20 in maize (Iijima et al., 2008) and 16 in rice plantlets (Wang et al., 2014a), in comparison to only 5 in Arabidopsis (Dolan et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2014a.

claim: Arabidopsis has only 5 cell layers in the columella.
source: This disparity can be explained by the presence of additional cell layers in the columella, with 20 in maize (Iijima et al., 2008) and 16 in rice plantlets (Wang et al., 2014a), in comparison to only 5 in Arabidopsis (Dolan et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dolan et al., 1993.

claim: Additional cell layers in the columella promote the formation of a slightly larger cap with more cell layers, but do not significantly increase the external surface in contact with the medium.
source: Although this promotes the formation of a slightly larger cap (see Lotus japonicus in Figure 4—figure supplement 1) with more cell layers, it does not significantly increase the external surface in contact with the medium.
evidence: This claim is inferred from anatomical considerations and observations in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pi interacts strongly with many cations.
source: Pi interacts strongly with many cations and exhibits a very weak diffusion coefficient in soil (from 10−12 to 10−15 m2 s−1; Schachtman et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schachtman et al., 1998.

claim: Pi exhibits a very weak diffusion coefficient in soil (from 10−12 to 10−15 m2 s−1).
source: Pi interacts strongly with many cations and exhibits a very weak diffusion coefficient in soil (from 10−12 to 10−15 m2 s−1; Schachtman et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schachtman et al., 1998.

claim: Pi mobility is very low.
source: Pi mobility is consequently very low, which promotes a Pi-depleted zone around the root as a result of its absorption by plants (Kanno et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the weak diffusion coefficient and supported by a citation to Kanno et al., 2012.

claim: Low Pi mobility promotes a Pi-depleted zone around the root as a result of its absorption by plants.
source: Pi mobility is consequently very low, which promotes a Pi-depleted zone around the root as a result of its absorption by plants (Kanno et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kanno et al., 2012.

claim: The root cap may provide a temporal advantage to the plant as the Pi stock available to the growing root becomes limited.
source: This suggests that the root cap may provide a temporal advantage to the plant (« first come, first served »), as the Pi stock available to the growing root becomes limited.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the ecological advantage of root cap Pi uptake.

claim: Root cap Pi uptake could be beneficial in natural soil with low Pi availability and high Pi heterogeneity.
source: This feature could therefore be beneficial in natural soil with low Pi availability and high Pi heterogeneity, which may explain the higher biomass gain observed in our soil experiments as compared to hydroponic conditions.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning connecting the temporal advantage to observed biomass gains.

claim: Gene expression studies have investigated the presence of ion transporters in the root cap for iron (IRT1).
source: Previous spatial gene expression studies have investigated the presence of ion transporters in the root cap for iron (IRT1; Vert et al., 2002), potassium (ATkT3/KUP4/TRH1; Vicente-Agullo et al., 2004), nitrate (NRT1-1; Remans et al., 2006) and boron (BOR1; Takano et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vert et al., 2002.

claim: Gene expression studies have investigated the presence of ion transporters in the root cap for potassium (ATkT3/KUP4/TRH1).
source: Previous spatial gene expression studies have investigated the presence of ion transporters in the root cap for iron (IRT1; Vert et al., 2002), potassium (ATkT3/KUP4/TRH1; Vicente-Agullo et al., 2004), nitrate (NRT1-1; Remans et al., 2006) and boron (BOR1; Takano et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vicente-Agullo et al., 2004.

claim: Gene expression studies have investigated the presence of ion transporters in the root cap for nitrate (NRT1-1).
source: Previous spatial gene expression studies have investigated the presence of ion transporters in the root cap for iron (IRT1; Vert et al., 2002), potassium (ATkT3/KUP4/TRH1; Vicente-Agullo et al., 2004), nitrate (NRT1-1; Remans et al., 2006) and boron (BOR1; Takano et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Remans et al., 2006.

claim: Gene expression studies have investigated the presence of ion transporters in the root cap for boron (BOR1).
source: Previous spatial gene expression studies have investigated the presence of ion transporters in the root cap for iron (IRT1; Vert et al., 2002), potassium (ATkT3/KUP4/TRH1; Vicente-Agullo et al., 2004), nitrate (NRT1-1; Remans et al., 2006) and boron (BOR1; Takano et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Takano et al., 2010.

claim: Accumulation of boron around the quiescent center was predicted using a model based on the distribution of several boron transporters.
source: For boron, accumulation of this element around the quiescent center was predicted using a model based on the distribution of several boron transporters (Takano et al., 2010) and confirmed by chemical analysis (Shimotohno et al., 2015), thereby indicating a role for the root tip in boron uptake.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Takano et al., 2010.

claim: Accumulation of boron around the quiescent center was confirmed by chemical analysis.
source: For boron, accumulation of this element around the quiescent center was predicted using a model based on the distribution of several boron transporters (Takano et al., 2010) and confirmed by chemical analysis (Shimotohno et al., 2015), thereby indicating a role for the root tip in boron uptake.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shimotohno et al., 2015.

claim: The root tip has a role in boron uptake.
source: For boron, accumulation of this element around the quiescent center was predicted using a model based on the distribution of several boron transporters (Takano et al., 2010) and confirmed by chemical analysis (Shimotohno et al., 2015), thereby indicating a role for the root tip in boron uptake.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the accumulation of boron around the quiescent center.

claim: Defects in the nitrate NRT1-1 carrier affect root morphology (gravitropism, modification of lateral root development, etc.).
source: Defects in the nitrate NRT1-1 (Krouk et al., 2010) or potassium TRH1 (Vicente-Agullo et al., 2004) carriers affect root morphology (gravitropism, modification of lateral root development, etc.).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krouk et al., 2010.

claim: Defects in the potassium TRH1 carrier affect root morphology (gravitropism, modification of lateral root development, etc.).
source: Defects in the nitrate NRT1-1 (Krouk et al., 2010) or potassium TRH1 (Vicente-Agullo et al., 2004) carriers affect root morphology (gravitropism, modification of lateral root development, etc.).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vicente-Agullo et al., 2004.

claim: NRT1-1 and TRH1 can competitively transport auxin.
source: This is related to the ability of these proteins to competitively transport auxin.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about these transporters.

claim: The presence of NRT1-1 and TRH1 in the root cap appears to be linked to a developmental role in the adaptation of root morphology to the presence of nitrate or potassium in the environment.
source: To date, their presence in the root cap appears to be linked to a developmental role in the adaptation of root morphology to the presence of nitrate or potassium in the environment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the effects of these transporters on root morphology.

claim: It is well documented that the primary root growth is disconnected from Pi import and Pi internal status.
source: In the case of Pi, it is well documented that the primary root growth is disconnected from Pi import and Pi internal status (for review see: Svistoonoff et al., 2007; Thibaud et al., 2010; Peret et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Svistoonoff et al., 2007; Thibaud et al., 2010; Peret et al., 2011.

claim: Pi absorption by the root cap has not been found to modify root architecture.
source: The present study confirms this view, as Pi absorption by the root cap has not been found to modify root architecture, although it significantly affects plant Pi nutrition.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the current study.

claim: Pi absorption by the root cap significantly affects plant Pi nutrition.
source: The present study confirms this view, as Pi absorption by the root cap has not been found to modify root architecture, although it significantly affects plant Pi nutrition.
evidence: This claim is based on data from the current study showing biomass gains and gene expression changes.

claim: For plantlets grown in vitro, a 20% increase in Pi uptake generated a 40% gain in biomass for the root tip-complemented line within 4 days.
source: Indeed for plantlets grown in vitro, a 20% increase in Pi uptake generated a 40% gain in biomass for the root tip-complemented line within 4 days.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: The level of Pi derived from root cap absorption contributed significantly to the modification of Pi homeostasis and to regulation of gene expression.
source: The level of Pi derived from root cap absorption (with regard to the size of this tissue) contributed also significantly to the modification of Pi homeostasis and to regulation of gene expression, as revealed by changes in the expression of several transcriptomic markers regulated by internal Pi status (Thibaud et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, and supported by a citation to Thibaud et al., 2010.

claim: Internal Pi may be involved in Pi homeostasis regulation.
source: This observation is in agreement with previous reports that internal Pi may be involved in Pi homeostasis regulation (Liu et al., 1998; Lv et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014b; Puga et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 1998; Lv et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014b; Puga et al., 2014.

claim: The transcriptional response was not linearly connected to Pi uptake.
source: The transcriptional response was not linearly connected to Pi uptake, since absorption in the root cap of the complemented line restored half of the regulation of Pi starvation systemic markers.
evidence: This claim is based on data showing non-proportional relationship between Pi uptake and gene expression changes.

claim: A small amount of Pi absorbed by the root at the root tip level can regulate gene expression in the whole plant.
source: As previously shown, this confirms that a small amount of Pi absorbed by the root (at the root tip level, as shown in this study) can regulate gene expression in the whole plant (Thibaud et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the current study and a citation to Thibaud et al., 2010.

claim: Charles Darwin characterized the root tip as a plant brain, based on its role in environmental perception and gravitropism.
source: Charles Darwin characterized the root tip as a plant brain, based on its role in environmental perception and gravitropism (Darwin and Darwin, 1880).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Darwin and Darwin, 1880.

claim: The root cap responds to various abiotic stresses including light.
source: Numerous studies since then have revealed how the root cap responds to various abiotic stresses including: light, modulation of root architecture in response to phosphate (Svistoonoff et al., 2007), and potassium or nitrate supply (Arnaud et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from multiple studies.

claim: The root cap responds to modulation of root architecture in response to phosphate.
source: Numerous studies since then have revealed how the root cap responds to various abiotic stresses including: light, modulation of root architecture in response to phosphate (Svistoonoff et al., 2007), and potassium or nitrate supply (Arnaud et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Svistoonoff et al., 2007.

claim: The root cap responds to potassium or nitrate supply.
source: Numerous studies since then have revealed how the root cap responds to various abiotic stresses including: light, modulation of root architecture in response to phosphate (Svistoonoff et al., 2007), and potassium or nitrate supply (Arnaud et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Arnaud et al., 2010.

claim: The root cap has essential roles in Pi nutrition.
source: The present study establishes essential roles for this tissue in Pi nutrition, as well as Pi homeostasis adaptation.
evidence: This claim is based on the findings of the current study.

claim: The root cap has essential roles in Pi homeostasis adaptation.
source: The present study establishes essential roles for this tissue in Pi nutrition, as well as Pi homeostasis adaptation.
evidence: This claim is based on the findings of the current study.

claim: The root cap contributes to the plant's adaptation to soil Pi presence in a disproportionate way, considering its diminutive size.
source: Finally, this study demonstrates that the root cap contributes to the plant's adaptation to soil Pi presence in a disproportionate way, considering its diminutive size.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the significant contribution of the small root cap to Pi uptake and plant growth.

claim: The diminutive size of the root cap cells at the root-to-soil exchange surface accounts for approximately 20% of the total seedling phosphate uptake.
source: Remarkably, the diminutive size of the root cap cells at the root-to-soil exchange surface accounts for a significant amount of the total seedling phosphate uptake (approximately 20%).
evidence: This claim is based on data from the complementation experiments.

claim: Root cap Pi absorption is sufficient for shoot biomass production (up to a 180% gain in soil).
source: This level of Pi absorption is sufficient for shoot biomass production (up to a 180% gain in soil), as well as repression of Pi starvation-induced genes.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Table 1.

claim: Root cap Pi absorption is sufficient for repression of Pi starvation-induced genes.
source: This level of Pi absorption is sufficient for shoot biomass production (up to a 180% gain in soil), as well as repression of Pi starvation-induced genes.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.
